content.title: If God chooses, do our choices and witness matter?
content.summary: Hold God’s sovereign grace together with real responsibility and the call to preach Christ.

answer.text: Yes. In the Reformed account, God’s choice is gracious and effective, while human choices remain real and morally accountable. He appoints the means as well as the end: people hear the gospel, repent and believe. Election gives no permission to neglect evangelism, excuse sin or decide that a particular neighbour is beyond the gospel’s reach.

reasoning.text: Paul locates election in God’s love and purpose before our achievements. Salvation gives grounds for gratitude, not a claim to superiority.
The cross joins God’s definite purpose with the guilt of those who crucified Jesus. Scripture does not treat divine purpose as erasing human responsibility.
God brings people to faith through the proclaimed gospel. Paul endures hardship for the elect so that they may obtain salvation; the doctrine energizes his mission.

conclusion.text: God’s sovereignty and the call to believe must be taught together. We proclaim Christ to everyone and trust God to give life through his Word and Spirit.

sections.text: Westminster and the Baptist confession of 1689 distinguish willing action from the fallen will’s spiritual bondage. The sinner acts willingly but cannot produce saving faith by unaided strength. In effectual calling, the Spirit renews the will so that the person comes freely to Christ. Grace changes the heart rather than dragging an unwilling believer into fellowship.
sections.title: What kind of freedom?

sections.text: The promise of John 6:37 directs us to Christ: the one who comes will not be cast out. A hearer need not first discover God’s secret decree. The revealed command is to repent and believe; the preacher’s task is to announce that promise truthfully.
sections.title: Begin with Christ’s invitation

sections.text: Baptists who hold the Reformed reading confess it in the Second London Confession (1677, reissued 1689), chapters 3 and 10, and many Southern Baptists hold it today, among them the Founders Ministries movement and Albert Mohler, president of the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary. Many other Southern Baptists do not. The convention's own confession, the Baptist Faith and Message 2000, says that election “is the gracious purpose of God, according to which He regenerates, justifies, sanctifies, and glorifies sinners. It is consistent with the free agency of man, and comprehends all the means in connection with the end” (article V), and leaves the details open. In 2012 Eric Hankins, a Mississippi pastor, drafted “A Statement of the Traditional Southern Baptist Understanding of God’s Plan of Salvation”, signed by former convention presidents including Jerry Vines and Paige Patterson. It denies “that election means that, from eternity, God predestined certain people for salvation and others for condemnation”, holds that Christ’s sacrifice is for “the sins of every person”, and denies that grace “cannot be resisted”. A 2013 report to the convention’s Executive Committee, “Truth, Trust, and Testimony in a Time of Tension”, asked both sides to work together in evangelism. Both affirm that God saves by grace through faith in Christ, that the gospel is to be offered to everyone, and that true believers are kept to the end.
sections.title: Where Baptists differ on election

content.objection: Is it unjust to hold people responsible if they cannot renew their own hearts?

reply.text: The Reformed answer distinguishes moral bondage from external compulsion: sinners act from their desires and remain responsible for their evil. Mercy is a gift, not a debt owed to otherwise innocent people. Romans 9 directly raises the objection and points to the Creator’s authority and mercy. That is a serious theological answer, while the relationship between sovereignty and responsibility still deserves patient examination.

limit.text: We cannot identify another person as reprobate or use election to excuse wrongdoing. God is not the author of sin. The doctrine is to be handled carefully, producing humility, obedience and consolation rather than speculation about hidden things.

prompt.text: When you say freedom, do you mean that a choice is willing, that it is morally good, or that God has no purpose governing it?
